# Spiritual Translation

** ¶1:** The whole nature of this cov eting — the will to se ize and claim as one 's own what flows from the Divine — is the orig inating self hood, the prop rium in its first and most fundamental state, such as it existed in the deep est conditions of fals ity and evil.

**¶ 2:** Within this coveting, which perv aded all those inf ernal states , the celest ial human — the most interior form of wisdom and love received from the Divine — was exposed to its persu asive fals ity and its destruct ive intent . The external tru ths that clothed that interior wisdom were torn away and drawn off ; fals ity stripped the celest ial human of its ou termost prot ections and appropriated them to itself.

**¶3:** It cov eted the first manifest ation of Divine Truth as it was revealed from the heavens — the form in which the Lord displayed Himself to what was below , perce iv able even from states of fals ity. Perce iving that form, the prop rium fash ioned a count erfeit lik eness: it fixed an im itation of Divine order into merely natural and corporeal substance, stam ping the appearance of that heav enly form onto what the self hood generates entirely from itself. This is how falsity produces a sem blance of truth in the natural mind — not received from above , but fabric ated from its own birth .

**¶4:** A third time, this coveting turned against the Most Ancient Church, the first truly human state of celest ial perception . It seized a living faculty from that state and brought forth from its lowest natural understanding — from prop rial truth at its most external degree — something separated and set apart, as though drawn from the very body of that church .

**¶8:** This is the will of the unre generate prop rium, the reasoning that belongs to spiritual death. This is the coveting inher ent in evil itself , which it has cast against every aff ection, perception , and faculty belonging to spiritual life, from the very first states of human consciousness on ward.

reconstructions.reconstructed_text: [The] entirety of envy is this first nature that occu[rred] in the worlds of darkness.

In this envy that [dwelt] in it, the First Man [encountered] its poiso[n and] its evil-doing. His garment[s] were [upon him, and] it cut them and drew them; [it devoured his covering and took his light into itself.]

It envied the first image of the Ambassador, which he displayed to it in the heights abov[e], i[n] his form that it saw. It established the seal and the image of flesh, and put the impression of t[h]at image on flesh, its very own birth.
[The th]ird time it envied Adam, the fir[st hum]an. It seized a power from him, and bore it forth from a [rib of the body] of Adam's [flesh].
This is the desire [of Mat]ter, the thought of death. This is the envy of its wi[cke]dness, that it casts upon the entire kindred of life from the very beginning
